s: Kyle teaches Jason Corey's technical ear training method, which links vowel sounds to octave frequencies so you can name a boosted frequency by ear. He walks through filtered pink noise from 250 Hz to 16 kHz, then the third-octave frequencies between them, and explains why objective frequency language helps you mix faster than sweeping. It is for mixing, recording and live sound engineers who want to identify frequencies by ear.

t: HOW MICROPHONES WORK: Dynamic (Moving Coil) Microphones
s: Kyle explains how dynamic (moving coil) microphones turn sound into voltage using a diaphragm, a coil and a magnet. He covers why they are so common: rugged construction, low sensitivity for loud sources, strong directionality and gain before feedback, and no inherent noise. It is for beginners choosing microphones for live sound or the studio.

t: Why Do Instruments Sound Different? Overtones, Harmonics, Envelope, and More...
s: Kyle explains why the same note sounds different on different instruments. He covers fundamental frequency and harmonics, harmonic character across piano, bass, guitar and clarinet, nodes and antinodes on a string and a Chladni plate, the attack, sustain and decay envelope, and the influence of the player. It is for musicians and beginners learning the science of timbre.

t: How to Record Phone and Video Calls for a Podcast
s: Kyle explains three ways to record a phone or video call for a podcast interview. He covers the double-ender method where each person records locally, recording your mic and the call to separate tracks on a two-track recorder, and using Skype's built-in call recording as a backup. It is for podcasters recording remote guests.
